paragraphs.heading: What palynology studies
paragraphs.text: Palynology is the study of microscopic organic remains found in sediments and sedimentary rocks. These remains are called palynomorphs. They include pollen and spores, and they are made of organic material that resists acid. They come from a wide range of plants, animals and Protista.

paragraphs.heading: Small and acid-proof
paragraphs.text: Palynomorphs range in size between 5 and 500 micrometres. They may be made of organic materials such as chitin and sporopollenin. They are taken out of soils, sedimentary rocks and sediment cores by a mix of physical steps, such as wet sieving, and a chemical step, acid digestion. Together these steps remove the non-organic part of the sample. Palynology does not cover diatoms or foraminiferans.

paragraphs.heading: A record of past life and climate
paragraphs.text: Palynomorphs form a geological record that helps show what kind of prehistoric life existed when a sedimentary layer was laid down. These microfossils therefore offer important clues to the climate that prevailed at the time. In paleoclimatology, fossil palynomorphs are studied as a way to reconstruct ancient environments and climates. They can be plentiful: organic marine deposits hold millions of palynomorphs per gram, even when such deposits generally do not bear fossils. In metamorphic or recrystallized rocks, however, they have generally been destroyed.

paragraphs.heading: Dating layers of rock
paragraphs.text: Palynology stands where earth science meets biology, particularly the science of plants. In biostratigraphy, fossil palynomorphs from the Precambrian to the Holocene are used to give relative dates to sedimentary layers and to correlate them. It is also a way to date many kinds of plants and animals and to understand their evolution.

paragraphs.heading: Honey, archaeology and the law
paragraphs.text: Archaeologists use palynology widely to reconstruct ancient environments and the environmental shifts that had a significant influence on past human societies. It is also used to reconstruct what prehistoric and historic people ate. Melissopalynology studies the pollen and other palynomorphs found in honey. It identifies where the pollen came from, both the geographical location and the genera of plants, and this is an important tool for discovering and policing honey that has been criminally adulterated or mislabeled. In forensic palynology, palynomorphs are evidence in civil and criminal law, used to prove or disprove that objects, people and places are physically linked.

paragraphs.heading: How pollen analysis spread
paragraphs.text: An 1888 study by Trybom looked at pollen samples from the sediments of Swedish lakes and found pine and spruce pollen in great quantity. Quantitative analysis of pollen began with the published work of Lennart von Post. The early investigations appeared in the Nordic languages, and because of that the field of pollen analysis stayed confined to those countries. That isolation ended when Gunnar Erdtman's 1921 thesis was published in German. The method became widespread across Europe and North America and revolutionized research on Quaternary vegetation and climate change.
